publisher: Bureau of Reclamation (US Department of the Interior)
title: Record of Decision, Decision Framework for Colorado River Guidelines: Coordinated Operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead (2027-2036)
date_evidence: Cover and running footer of the Record of Decision read: August 2026. Signing date of 21 August 2026 is documented in the Department of the Interior release issued the same day (meta-dcterms.date: 2026-08-21).
key_claim: The decision adopts a 2027-2036 Decision Framework of operational principles and sideboards rather than fixed allocations, with Operating Guidelines anticipated to be issued for two-year intervals, and records that the seven Basin States have not reached consensus.
frame_summary: Reclamation is arguing that with no seven-state consensus available, the Secretary's authority exercised through a deliberately adaptive, open-ended framework is the legitimate instrument of river governance, and that flexibility is a feature rather than a failure to decide.
verbatim_quote: Operating intervals are anticipated to be of 2-year lengths, unless consensus-based agreements or other conditions warrant otherwise.
verbatim_list: The decision is the approval of the following Federal action: the adoption of the 2027–2036 Decision Framework, as provided in Section 10, that establishes the operational principles, sideboards (ranges for operational elements) and a process to govern development and issuance of Operating Guidelines for the coordinated operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead.
The Decision Framework shall remain in effect through operating year 2036 unless superseded by subsequent Federal action.

At the time of this ROD, the seven Basin States have not reached a consensus on an operational approach to the coordinated operations of Lake Powell and Lake Mead, and the Lower Division States are developing but have not yet reached agreement on several matters related to the operations of Lake Mead.
Unfortunately, as of the publication of this Record of Decision (ROD), consensus on long-term operations has not been reached.
notes: Primary anchor. The two-year interval is the mechanism this scan is about. The ROD itself contains no per-state acre-foot figures; those sit in the separate Operating Guidelines and the Interior release.

title: Interior Department Finalizes Plans for 2027-2028 Colorado River Operations
key_claim: Lower Basin deliveries are reduced by 1.25 million acre-feet in each of the next two years, with a proposed state split of Arizona 760,000, California 440,000 and Nevada 50,000 acre-feet, plus at least 700,000 acre-feet of voluntary conservation over the two-year period.
frame_summary: Interior is arguing that the outcome is collaborative water management preserved rather than consensus failed, presenting the two-year cycle and the retained room for voluntary agreement as stewardship rather than as an inability to set durable rules.
verbatim_quote: The Decision Framework anticipates operating guidelines in two-year periods and can be scaled longer depending on evolving Basin circumstances.
verbatim_list: Provides for reductions in deliveries of Colorado River water among the Lower Basin States of 1.25 million acre-feet in each year of the next two years.

Provide for Lower Basin States to voluntarily conserve and store at least 700,000 acre-feet of water over the two-year period to protect the system, in addition to the 1.25 million acre-feet per year of reductions.

The Decision Framework establishes an operational range that provides the flexibility to develop specific operating guidelines within the 10-year period while preserving the opportunity for Colorado River Basin negotiations to continue and, if successful, be incorporated into years three or four or longer for future operational guidelines.
For Lake Mead, water deliveries to the Lower Basin States will be reduced by 1.25 million-acre feet for calendar year 2027.
Arizona: 760,000 acre-feet
California: 440,000 acre-feet
Nevada: 50,000 acre-feet

publisher: Bureau of Reclamation (US Department of the Interior)
title: Reclamation and Interior finalise post-2026 Colorado River operations, news release 5392
key_claim: Combined Lake Powell and Lake Mead contents are the lowest since before Lake Powell began filling in 1963, both reservoirs hit record lows in the weeks before the decision, and the river sustains 5.5 million acres of farmland.
frame_summary: Reclamation is arguing that hydrological emergency justifies an adaptive federal framework over a fixed long-term allocation, positioning the agency as a facilitator that keeps space open for state-led consensus and voluntary conservation.
verbatim_quote: The combined contents of Lake Powell and Lake Mead have not been this low since before Lake Powell began filling following the closure of the gates at Glen Canyon Dam in 1963, with both Lake Powell and Lake Mead hitting record lows the last few weeks.
verbatim_list: It serves as a vital resource for 30 tribes and two Mexican states, sustaining 5.5 million acres of farmland and agricultural communities throughout the West, while also supporting critical ecosystems and protecting endangered species.

Lake Powell will begin the October 1 water year between elevations 3,540 and 3,510 feet, placing operations in the Lower Elevation Infrastructure Protection Range with an expected water year release between 6.0 and 7.0 million acre-feet.

publisher: Arizona Water News (Arizona Department of Water Resources)
title: Statement on Reclamation's Record of Decision and Operating Guidelines for future Colorado River operations
key_claim: Arizona's state water regulator treats the 2027-2028 guidelines as stability achieved for two years while stating that the framework for years three to ten remains a concern and the subject of continued negotiation.
frame_summary: ADWR is arguing that the two-year deal is hard-won stability that buys negotiating time without conceding Arizona's legal rights, framing the unresolved years three to ten as the real contest still ahead.
verbatim_quote: While the framework for years 3-10 continues to be of concern, we applaud the Department of the Interior for clarifying the decision-making process for operations beyond 2028.
verbatim_list: After more than three years of difficult negotiations over post-2026 Colorado River Operations guidelines, Arizona and the Lower Basin states have created a level of stability for the Colorado River system with the adoption of the 2027-2028 operating guidelines in the Record of Decision.

publisher: Know Your Water News (Central Arizona Project)
title: Record of Decision and Operating Guidelines underscore need for 3-state deal
key_claim: The Central Arizona Project reads the two-year guidelines as certainty for two years only, and rejects the post-2028 framework in the Record of Decision as containing conditions it will not accept.
frame_summary: CAP is arguing that the two-year window is a reprieve rather than a settlement, and that the federal post-2028 framework shifts burden unlawfully onto Arizona, so the decision increases rather than reduces the pressure to reach a three-state deal.
verbatim_quote: CAP supports the finalization and implementation of a Lower Basin proposal to provide water certainty for the next two years.
verbatim_list: The 2026-2028 Operating Guidelines contemplate the execution and incorporation of a Lower Basin states agreement that would conserve at least 3.2 million acre-feet of Lower Basin states' water through 2028 and may provide the time needed to negotiate a long-term resolution to the River's future outside protracted litigation.
As written, the post-2028 framework described in the Record of Decision includes conditions which CAP will not accept, but there will be time to negotiate that over the next two years.

title: Colorado River states can't agree, so California is poised for more cuts
key_claim: Water infrastructure takes decades and billions of dollars to build, and without longer-term certainty about how the river is shared, cities and irrigation providers cannot plan; California faces roughly a 10% cut, about 440,000 acre-feet a year, through 2028.
frame_summary: CalMatters is arguing that the damaging feature of the federal approach is the two-year planning horizon itself rather than the size of any single cut, because rolling short-term rules paralyse the multi-decade permitting, conservation and infrastructure decisions that closing the gap requires.
verbatim_quote: Building anything to store, move or make more water typically takes decades and billions of dollars.
verbatim_list: These dramatic cuts are an upper limit for future operations: The federal government plans to roll out more detailed management plans every two years if the states continue their impasse.

The agency will release the first of those plans any day, imposing cuts in the downstream states of California, Arizona and Nevada — an estimated 10% cut to California's supply through 2028, or roughly 440,000 acre-feet a year.

California uses the largest share of the Colorado River's water among the states. And the Imperial Irrigation District uses the largest share of that to supply half a million acres of alfalfa, grasses, winter vegetables and other crops in the southeast corner of the state.
Seeking those permits and environmental approvals "needs to be done on a longer term, not on a two-year term," Shields said.

title: Interior Department finalizes new Colorado River operating rules for 2027-2028
key_claim: Approximately 470,000 acres of Imperial Valley farmland depend on Colorado River water, and the open question for growers is how much of California's 440,000 acre-foot annual reduction falls on the Imperial Irrigation District.
frame_summary: The Desert Review is arguing that the federal decision settles the volumetric question while relocating the distributional fight, leaving the exposure of senior-priority agriculture unresolved and therefore unplannable.
verbatim_quote: Approximately 470,000 acres of highly productive farmland depend on Colorado River water, supporting agricultural production that supplies a substantial portion of the nation's winter vegetables.
verbatim_list: For Imperial Valley farmers, the most consequential provision may be the requirement for the Lower Basin states — Arizona, California and Nevada — to reduce Colorado River deliveries by 1.25 million acre-feet in each of the next two years.

For Imperial Valley farmers, however, the central issue remains straightforward: how much of California's 440,000-acre-foot annual reduction will ultimately come from the Imperial Irrigation District's water supply?
